prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets

statement.case_for: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices (Berry 1994; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995), together with Pakes's dynamic oligopoly and estimation work, made empirical industrial organisation quantitative and credible. It is a method and a framework at once: it lets analysts recover realistic substitution patterns and market power from market data. It is now used in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and in trade, health and environmental applications, so its reach goes well beyond one subfield. The core papers are about three decades old, so replication, critique and extension are extensive and timing is not an issue. The three-name attribution is compact: BLP is the clear centre of the demand-estimation breakthrough, and Pakes anchors the dynamic-industry strand. After reading colleagues' openings, my view is unchanged. B012 is the candidate in which the link between theory and data and the breadth of downstream use are strongest, and its attribution is cleaner than the most crowded alternatives such as B043.
statement.case_against: The three-name limit leaves out contributors whom several colleagues and I regard as real: Bresnahan (earlier empirical IO foundations), Reiss, Benkard and Levin. A citation centred on demand estimation understates Pakes's dynamic-games work. A committee could also weigh structural methodology below a substantive discovery. B002 has much broader opening support and a very clean two-author attribution, which makes it a serious rival. My own preference may be shaped by my affinity for tractable methods that are carried into practice.

responses.point: Ranks B012 first, regards BLP as the clean core with Pakes as anchor, and asks whether Bresnahan should be included. Also notes that the field has no earlier laureate for empirical IO, so field priority is uncertain.
responses.response: I agree that BLP with Pakes as anchor is the cleanest attribution, and I keep Bresnahan out of the preferred part because his contribution is earlier and more separable from the specific demand-estimation breakthrough. I would qualify the point about field priority: I cannot independently verify that no earlier prize touched this area, and field novelty should not count as merit. I would rest the case on methodological reach, durability and attribution clarity.

responses.point: Regards BLP as a compact, well-identified three-person contribution, with Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin more peripheral. Also asks whether the Committee treats this as an IO or an econometrics contribution.
responses.response: I agree on the compactness of the BLP core. On classification, I think the question matters less than it seems: the contribution is a method that changed what empirical work in IO, trade and policy can do. The cost of the cap is real, though. Benkard and Levin belong to the dynamic-game strand, which a demand-focused citation does not capture, and I do not want to understate that.

responses.point: Ranks B002 first and proposes Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler, centring the award on collateral constraints while recognising Gertler's accelerator work. Acknowledges that Bernanke's 2022 recognition and the 2022 banking prize limit the room for the accelerator strand.
responses.response: I rank B002 third and take the argument seriously. Kiyotaki-Moore is the clearest origin of the mechanism, and I would credit it to the two originators. Adding Gertler seems to me to blur the citation, because his accelerator work builds on a lineage that includes an existing laureate, and Gertler also appears under B043. If the Committee chose B002, I would prefer Kiyotaki and Moore alone. I do not think support for B002 settles the merit comparison with B012.

responses.point: Proposes Rubinstein alone for B001, because Wolinsky and Binmore are more derivative, and notes that game theory may face a higher threshold.
responses.response: I accept that the 1982 result is Rubinstein's alone and that the field threshold is a fair worry. Where I differ is that the Rubinstein-Wolinsky market-bargaining work is a distinct, widely used contribution and not a mere extension, so I would keep it as an option for a two-name credit. That is part of why B001 stays an alternative and not my preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would rather credit Bresnahan, or a wider 'new empirical IO' group, than the three BLP authors.
Whether a demand-estimation citation sufficiently reflects Pakes's dynamic-game contributions without crediting Benkard and Levin.
How the Committee weighs methodological tools against substantive discovery when comparing B012 with B002.
My recollection of relative credit within the structural-IO group, and of whether any earlier prize covered this area, is not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile shows no co-authorship or institutional link to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn or the other B012 names. My work on matching, auctions and market design is a field adjacency, not a personal connection.
